title: How do you centralize logs across many services/containers (ELK/EFK, Loki), and how do you trace a single request end-to-end across services (correlation/trace ID propagation, OpenTelemetry, Jaeger/Zipkin)?
shortTitle: Centralizing logs across many services/containers (ELK/EFK, Loki) and tracing a single request end-to-end (correlation ID, OpenTelemetry, Jaeger/Zipkin)

s1_definition.profdef: Centralizing logs means every service and container writes structured logs that are shipped by a collector to a single searchable store, so you query all logs in one place instead of SSH-ing into each host. The ELK stack uses Elasticsearch for storage, Logstash or Beats for shipping, and Kibana for search; EFK swaps Logstash for Fluentd or Fluent Bit; Loki stores logs cheaply indexed by labels and is queried with LogQL in Grafana. Distributed tracing follows a single request across services by generating a trace id at the edge and propagating it through every call via headers, with each service recording spans; OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral instrumentation standard and Jaeger or Zipkin store and visualize the traces.
s1_definition.analogy: When a transfer from Rajesh SAV2001 to Priya CUR3001 passes through five different departments at the National Bank of India, each department used to keep its own private diary on its own desk. If something went wrong, an investigator had to physically visit all five desks. Centralized logging is like photocopying every department's diary entry and filing it in one central records room that anyone can search instantly. Distributed tracing adds a single case number stamped on the transfer form the moment it enters the building, and every department writes that same case number in its diary. Now the investigator searches the central room for one case number and instantly sees the complete journey across all five departments in order.
s1_definition.oneliner: Ship every service's structured logs to one searchable store, and stamp every request with a propagated trace id so you can reconstruct its whole cross-service journey.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Centralizing logs means every service and container writes structured logs that are shipped by a collector to a single searchable store, so you query all logs in one place instead of SSH-ing into each host. The ELK stack uses Elasticsearch for storage, Logstash or Beats for shipping, and Kibana for search; EFK swaps Logstash for Fluentd or Fluent Bit; Loki stores logs cheaply indexed by labels and is queried with LogQL in Grafana. Distributed tracing follows a single request across services by generating a trace id at the edge and propagating it through every call via headers, with each service recording spans; OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral instrumentation standard and Jaeger or Zipkin store and visualize the traces.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When a transfer from Rajesh SAV2001 to Priya CUR3001 passes through five different departments at the National Bank of India, each department used to keep its own private diary on its own desk. If something went wrong, an investigator had to physically visit all five desks. Centralized logging is like photocopying every department's diary entry and filing it in one central records room that anyone can search instantly. Distributed tracing adds a single case number stamped on the transfer form the moment it enters the building, and every department writes that same case number in its diary. Now the investigator searches the central room for one case number and instantly sees the complete journey across all five departments in order.

**One line to remember:** Ship every service's structured logs to one searchable store, and stamp every request with a propagated trace id so you can reconstruct its whole cross-service journey.

sections.s2_technical:
Centralized logging starts with structured logs. Instead of free-text lines, each service emits JSON with consistent fields: a timestamp, a level, a service name, a message, and context fields including the trace id. Structured logs are machine-parseable, so the store can index and filter them. In a containerized world, applications write logs to standard output, and a collector running on each node — Fluent Bit or Filebeat as a DaemonSet in Kubernetes — tails the container log files, enriches them with pod and namespace metadata, and ships them onward.

The storage and query layer is where ELK, EFK, and Loki differ. Elasticsearch indexes the full content of every log, which makes arbitrary text search powerful but storage-heavy and expensive at scale; Kibana is its search UI. EFK is the same idea with Fluentd or Fluent Bit as the shipper, common in Kubernetes. Loki takes a deliberately cheaper approach: it indexes only a small set of labels (service, namespace, level) and stores the log bodies compressed, so you filter by label first and then grep within, which is far cheaper but less suited to arbitrary full-text search. Loki is queried with LogQL inside Grafana, which pairs naturally with Prometheus metrics in the same UI. You choose based on cost and search needs: Loki for cost-efficient label-scoped search, Elasticsearch when you need rich full-text analytics.

Distributed tracing solves a different problem: a single request touches many services, and you need to see its full path. The mechanism is a trace context. At the edge — the API gateway or the first service — a trace id is generated, a unique id for the whole request. Each unit of work within a service is a span with its own span id and a parent span id, forming a tree. The crucial step is propagation: when service A calls service B, it passes the trace context in HTTP headers, using the W3C Trace Context standard header `traceparent`. Service B reads that header, continues the same trace, and creates child spans. Without propagation, you would get disconnected fragments instead of one connected trace.

OpenTelemetry is the industry-standard, vendor-neutral way to instrument all of this. Its SDKs and auto-instrumentation libraries generate spans for incoming and outgoing HTTP calls, database queries, and messaging, and inject and extract the trace headers automatically. The spans are exported through the OpenTelemetry Collector to a backend such as Jaeger or Zipkin, which stores them and renders the waterfall view showing each service's span, its duration, and any errors. The final piece is correlation between logs and traces: you put the trace id into the logging context, typically the MDC in a Java application, so every log line carries the trace id. Then from a trace in Jaeger you pivot straight to the logs for that exact trace id in Loki or Kibana.

A senior nuance: tracing every request is expensive, so you sample — tail-based sampling keeps all traces that contain an error or exceed a latency threshold while sampling only a fraction of the fast successful ones, which keeps cost down without losing the interesting traces. You also standardize field names across services so searches work uniformly, and you never log secrets or full PII — account ids are fine as identifiers, but passwords and full card numbers are redacted. And you set retention tiers: hot storage for recent logs you query often, cheaper cold storage for older logs kept for compliance.
sections.s3_banking:
A transfer at the National Bank of India from Rajesh SAV2001 to Priya CUR3001 passes through an API gateway, a transfer service, a fraud service, and a notification service — four separate containers. A transfer fails intermittently and the on-call engineer must investigate.

Problem 1 — Each service logs to its own container, so the engineer cannot see the whole picture. The fix is centralized logging: every service emits structured JSON to standard output, a collector ships it to a central store, and the engineer searches one place.

Problem 2 — Even with central logs, the engineer cannot tell which log lines belong to the SAME failed transfer out of thousands happening concurrently. The fix is a trace id generated at the gateway and propagated through every service, written into every log line.

Problem 3 — The engineer needs to see where the time went and which hop failed. The fix is spans recorded per service and assembled into a trace waterfall.

Our runnable Java simulation models the trace context propagation: a `TraceContext` carrying a trace id, a `Service` base behaviour that logs with the trace id and records a span, four services chained together passing the context, and a `CentralLogStore` that collects every service's structured log so we can "search by trace id" at the end. Classes: `TraceContext`, `Span`, `CentralLogStore`, `TransferPipeline` (gateway, transfer, fraud, notify), and a `TracingDemo` main.

##### 4c. Configuration Files — the log shipper and JSON logging

```yaml
# k8s/fluent-bit-daemonset.yaml — one shipper per node tails container stdout
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: fluent-bit
  namespace: logging
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: fluent-bit }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: fluent-bit }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: fluent-bit
          image: fluent/fluent-bit:2.2
          volumeMounts:
            - name: varlog
              mountPath: /var/log           # tails all container logs
      volumes:
        - name: varlog
          hostPath: { path: /var/log }
```

```xml
<!-- logback-spring.xml — structured JSON logs; traceId pulled from MDC for correlation -->
<configuration>
  <appender name="JSON" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
    <encoder class="net.logstash.logback.encoder.LogstashEncoder">
      <includeMdcKeyName>traceId</includeMdcKeyName>  <!-- correlate logs with traces -->
      <customFields>{"service":"${SERVICE_NAME}"}</customFields>
    </encoder>
  </appender>
  <root level="INFO"><appender-ref ref="JSON"/></root>
</configuration>
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -cp target/classes com.bank.trace.TracingDemo

# Real stack:
kubectl apply -f k8s/fluent-bit-daemonset.yaml        # ship logs to Loki/Elasticsearch
# Run Jaeger all-in-one for traces:
docker run -d -p 16686:16686 -p 4317:4317 jaegertracing/all-in-one:1.54
# Auto-instrument a Spring Boot service with OpenTelemetry (no code changes):
java -javaagent:opentelemetry-javaagent.jar \
     -Dotel.service.name=transfer-service \
     -Dotel.exporter.otlp.endpoint=http://localhost:4317 \
     -jar transfer-service.jar
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: a single transfer of 50000 rupees from Rajesh SAV2001 to Priya CUR3001 entering the API gateway.

Step 1: The API gateway is the edge, so it generates a brand new trace id for this request and writes its first structured log line carrying that trace id. The line is shipped to the central store, and a gateway span is recorded.

Step 2: The gateway calls the transfer service, passing the trace context. The transfer service continues the same trace id, logs that it validated Rajesh's balance, ships that log, and records its span. Because the trace id is identical, these lines are now linked to the gateway line.

Step 3: The transfer service calls the fraud service, propagating the trace context in what would be a header. The fraud service continues the same trace id, scores the risk as low, and ships its log line and span under the same trace id.

Step 4: The transfer service debits Rajesh and credits Priya, logging that step, then calls the notification service, which sends the SMS and ships its log under the same trace id. All four services have now contributed log lines and spans sharing one trace id.

Step 5: The engineer searches the central store for that single trace id and instantly gets the complete ordered journey across all four services, even though thousands of other transfers were running at the same time. The trace waterfall shows the fraud service took the most time, pinpointing where attention is needed.

  └──────────────────┘  └──────────────────┘

  [NO_CONTEXT] ──gateway newTrace()──→ [TRACE_STARTED]
                                            │ pass traceparent header
                                            ▼

                                            ▼

  2.   → ctx = TraceContext.newTrace()  (gateway, edge)
  3.   → transferService(ctx,...)       continue same traceId
  4.     → fraudService(ctx,...)         continue same traceId
  5.     → notifyService(ctx,...)        continue same traceId

sections.s6_takeaway:
Centralizing logs means every service and container emits structured JSON logs to standard output, a collector such as Fluent Bit or Filebeat running as a DaemonSet on each node tails those logs, enriches them with pod and namespace metadata, and ships them to one searchable store. The ELK stack uses Elasticsearch for storage with Kibana as the UI and gives rich full-text search but is storage-heavy; EFK swaps in Fluentd or Fluent Bit as the shipper; and Loki takes a cheaper approach by indexing only a few labels and compressing the log bodies, queried with LogQL in Grafana. I choose based on cost and search needs, but the goal is always the same: one place to search instead of logging into every host.

Tracing a single request end-to-end is a different problem solved by trace context propagation. At the edge, the API gateway or first service generates a unique trace id for the whole request. Each unit of work becomes a span with a span id and a parent, and the crucial step is propagation — when one service calls another it passes the trace context in the W3C traceparent HTTP header, and the downstream service continues the same trace. OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard that auto-instruments incoming and outgoing calls, injects and extracts those headers, and exports spans to Jaeger or Zipkin, which draw the waterfall showing each service's duration and any errors.

The two come together through correlation. I put the trace id into the logging context, the MDC in a Java service, so every log line carries the trace id, and then from a trace in Jaeger I can pivot straight to the logs for that exact trace id. In my project at the National Bank of India, a transfer from Rajesh's SAV2001 to Priya's CUR3001 passed through the gateway, the transfer service, the fraud service, and the notification service — four separate containers. When a transfer failed intermittently, I searched the central log store for the one trace id and instantly saw the complete ordered journey across all four services, even among thousands of concurrent transfers, and the trace waterfall showed the fraud service was the slow hop. To control cost I use tail-based sampling that keeps every error trace and every slow trace but only a fraction of the fast successful ones, and I never log secrets or full card numbers. The principle I always state is that centralized structured logs give you one place to look and a propagated trace id gives you the thread that stitches a single request's whole journey together.
